literal: When Xuanzong was crown prince he attended Empress You every three days; she caressed and remembered him with added motherly love.
idiomatic: As crown prince Xuanzong visited Empress You every three days; she doted on him with growing affection.

literal: When Gaozu campaigned, Xuanzong entering court always stayed long in the inner palace; she personally watched his combing and bathing—motherly conduct in full measure.
idiomatic: On Gaozu's campaigns Xuanzong would linger in the inner palace, where she personally attended his grooming—her motherhood complete.

literal: Later the authorities memorialized to add the zhaoyi title; her posthumous name was Worthy Lady Wenzhao, and Gaozu assented.
idiomatic: Later officials petitioned to grant her the zhaoyi title posthumously as Worthy Lady Wenzhao, and Gaozu agreed.

literal: When Xuanzong ascended the throne, she was honored posthumously with joint offerings.
idiomatic: When Xuanzong took the throne, she was posthumously honored with joint temple sacrifice.

literal: The empress had first been buried southeast of Changling outside the western city; the tomb precinct was low and cramped.
idiomatic: She had first been buried southeast of Changling outside the west wall, in a modest tomb layout.

literal: A hill tomb was therefore raised on the spot, named Zhongning Mausoleum, with five hundred householders for the fief.
idiomatic: A hill tomb was raised there, named Zhongning Mausoleum, with a fief of five hundred households.

literal: Emperor Xiaozong edicted: "Grand Empress Dowager Wenzhao—her virtue matched earth's measure, her beauty echoed Wen Jiang; united with Gaozu she truly bore a sage, yet her early death dimmed her light and her lonely mound was not joined.
idiomatic: Emperor Xiaozong decreed: "Grand Empress Dowager Wenzhao matched earth in virtue and Wen Jiang in grace; wed to Gaozu she bore a sage, yet she died young and her lonely mound was not joined in sacrifice.

literal: The late emperor's filial feeling came from the heart; the transfer of her remains was not completed—endless grief and resentment, righteousness binding the hidden and the bright.
idiomatic: The late emperor's filial heart could not finish moving her; grief binds the living and the dead.

literal: Deposing Lü and honoring Bo, the rites of Han were fulfilled.
idiomatic: As Han deposed Lü and honored Bo, so shall rite be restored.

literal: " Another edict said: "Grand Empress Dowager Wenzhao, honored with Gaozu, enshrined in the temple with title fixed—hasten the transfer of her remains; from end to beginning the empress dowager shall preside. She may further be elevated to Grand Empress Dowager, matching Han and Jin precedent and rectifying mother-in-law and daughter-in-law rites.
idiomatic: " A second decree said: "Grand Empress Dowager Wenzhao is to be honored with Gaozu, enshrined, and moved at once; from first to last the empress dowager shall preside. Raise her title to Grand Empress Dowager, as in Han and Jin, to set mother-in-law and daughter-in-law rites aright.

literal: Her temple title remains as before.
idiomatic: Her temple title remains unchanged.

literal: " Wenzhao's spirit coffin was moved sixty paces northwest of Changling's precinct.
idiomatic: " Her coffin was moved sixty paces northwest of Changling's mound.

literal: When Zhongning Mausoleum was first opened several zhang deep, on the outer coffin a great serpent more than a zhang long was found, black, with the character "king" on its head, coiled and motionless.
idiomatic: When the tomb was opened several zhang deep, a black serpent over a zhang long was found on the coffin, the character "king" on its head, coiled and still.

literal: After the spirit coffin was moved, the serpent was placed back in its former spot.
idiomatic: After the move the serpent was returned to its place.

literal: Empress Shun of Emperor Xuanwu, the Yu clan, was a daughter of Lie's younger brother Jin.
idiomatic: Empress Shun of Emperor Xuanwu, née Yu, was a daughter of Jin, younger brother of Grand Commandant Lie.

literal: When Xuanzong first personally handled government, Lie was then director of the guards, holding the core trust; as consorts were not yet complete, through attendants' persuasion they praised the empress's looks and virtue, and Xuanzong welcomed her in as noble lady.
idiomatic: When Xuanzong began to rule in person, Lie commanded the guards; attendants praised the empress's grace, and Xuanzong took her in as a noble lady.

literal: She was fourteen, greatly favored, installed as empress, and presented at the imperial temple.
idiomatic: At fourteen she was deeply favored, made empress, and presented at the ancestral temple.

literal: The empress was quiet, forbearing, and not jealous; she bore Prince Chang, who died at three.
idiomatic: Quiet and tolerant, not jealous, she bore Prince Chang, who died at three.

literal: Later she died suddenly; palace affairs were secret and none could know fully, yet public opinion blamed Lady Gao.
idiomatic: She then died suddenly; palace matters were secret, but opinion blamed Lady Gao.

literal: She was buried at Yongtai Mausoleum with posthumous title Empress Shun.
idiomatic: She was buried at Yongtai Mausoleum as Empress Shun.

literal: Empress of Emperor Xuanwu, the Gao clan, was a daughter of Wenzhao Empress's younger brother Yan.
idiomatic: Empress of Emperor Xuanwu, née Gao, was a daughter of Wenzhao Empress's brother Yan.

literal: Xuanzong took her in as noble lady; she bore a prince who died young, and also Princess Jiande.
idiomatic: Xuanzong took her as noble lady; a prince died young, then she bore Princess Jiande.

literal: Later she was appointed empress and was greatly honored.
idiomatic: She was later made empress and held in high esteem.

literal: By nature jealous, palace women rarely gained access to the emperor.
idiomatic: Jealous by nature, she kept other women from the emperor's bed.

literal: When Xiaozong ascended the throne, she was given the exalted title Empress Dowager.
idiomatic: When Xiaozong took the throne she was made empress dowager.

literal: Soon she became a nun, dwelling at Yaoguang Temple; except for great festivals she did not enter the palace.
idiomatic: She soon took the veil at Yaoguang Temple and entered the palace only on great occasions.

literal: Princess Jiande, only five or six, Empress Dowager Ling always kept at her side and cherished her.
idiomatic: Princess Jiande, five or six years old, Empress Dowager Ling kept always beside her and cherished her.

literal: In the first year of Shengui the empress dowager went out to visit her mother Lady of Wuyi.
idiomatic: In Shengui year 1 the empress dowager went to visit her mother, Lady of Wuyi.

literal: Heavenly signs were then in flux; Empress Dowager Ling wished the empress to bear the calamity; that night she died suddenly, and the realm deemed it unjust.
idiomatic: Omens were abroad; Empress Dowager Ling meant the empress to take the blame; that night she died suddenly, and the realm cried injustice.

literal: The funeral returned to Yaoguang Buddhist Temple; burial of consorts all followed nun rites.
idiomatic: Her funeral was at Yaoguang Temple, with nun rites as for a consort.

literal: At first, during Gaozu's favor for Empress You, he wished to keep his love exclusive; access in the inner palace was often blocked.
idiomatic: When Gaozu favored Empress You he sought exclusive love and often barred the inner palace.

literal: Gaozu once told close ministers that women's jealousy and guarding—even kings cannot escape it, how much more commoners?
idiomatic: Gaozu once told his intimates that even kings cannot escape a woman's jealousy—how much less common men?

literal: In Xuanzong's later years Empress Gao was fierce and jealous; ladies and concubines included some who until the emperor's death never received him.
idiomatic: In Xuanzong's last years Empress Gao was fierce; some consorts never saw the emperor until his death.

literal: Thus in two reigns at Luoyang, for more than twenty years, the only prince raised whole was Xiaozong alone.
idiomatic: Thus through two reigns at Luoyang, for over twenty years, only Xiaozong among princes was raised to adulthood.

literal: Empress Ling of Emperor Xuanwu, the Hu clan, was a native of Linjing in Anding, daughter of Minister of Education Guozhen.
idiomatic: Empress Ling of Emperor Xuanwu, née Hu, came from Linjing in Anding, daughter of Minister of Education Guozhen.

literal: Her mother was the Huangfu clan; on the day the empress was born, red light shone on all sides.
idiomatic: Her mother was of the Huangfu clan; on her birth day red light filled the room.

literal: In Shangbei county of Jingzhao there was Zhao Hu, skilled in divination and physiognomy; Guozhen questioned him.
idiomatic: Zhao Hu of Shangbei in Jingzhao, skilled in divination, was consulted by Guozhen.

literal: Hu said: "Your worthy daughter bears the marks of great nobility; she will become mother of heaven and earth and bear the lord of heaven and earth.
idiomatic: Hu said: "This worthy daughter shows supreme nobility; she will be mother of the realm and bear its lord.

literal: Let no more than three persons know.
idiomatic: Let no more than three know of this.

literal: " The empress's aunt was a nun, quite able to expound the Way; at the beginning of Xuanzong's reign she entered the forbidden precinct to lecture.
idiomatic: " Her aunt was a nun skilled in doctrine who entered the palace early in Xuanzong's reign to lecture.

literal: After several years attendants were prompted to praise the empress's looks and conduct; Xuanzong heard and summoned her to the inner palace as Shining Splendor world-lady.
idiomatic: For years attendants praised her grace; Xuanzong heard and summoned her to the inner palace as Shining Splendor attendant.

literal: Yet in the pepper chambers, by the state's old custom, they prayed together, all wishing to bear princes and princesses, not wishing to bear the crown prince.
idiomatic: By old custom women of the inner palace prayed together to bear princes or princesses, not the crown prince.

literal: Only the empress often told the ladies: "Can the Son of Heaven truly have no son? Why fear one's own death and leave the imperial house without its legitimate heir?
idiomatic: Only she told the ladies: "Can the Son of Heaven have no son? Why fear death and leave the house without its heir?

literal: " When Xiaozong was in her womb, her peers still frightened her with precedent and urged various schemes.
idiomatic: " When she carried Xiaozong, her peers still frightened her with precedent and urged schemes against it.

literal: The empress's resolve was firm; in the dark night she vowed alone: "If what I carry is a boy and by order he should be eldest son, though bearing him costs my life I will not refuse.
idiomatic: She was resolute; in the dark she vowed alone: "If it is a boy and he is to be heir, I accept death in giving birth.

literal: " After Xiaozong was born she was advanced to Full Splendor concubine.
idiomatic: " After Xiaozong was born she was made Full Splendor concubine.

literal: Before this Xuanzong had frequently lost princes; considering himself advanced in years, he guarded them deeply.
idiomatic: Xuanzong had lost many sons; feeling his years advance, he guarded infants strictly.

literal: Wet nurses were chosen, all from good families suited to bear sons.
idiomatic: He chose wet nurses from good families known for bearing sons.

literal: They were raised in a separate palace; neither the empress nor the Full Splendor concubine might nurse or see them.
idiomatic: They were reared in a separate palace; neither empress nor concubine might rear or see them.

literal: When Xiaozong ascended the throne, she was first honored as imperial consort dowager, then as empress dowager.
idiomatic: When Xiaozong took the throne she was first grand imperial consort, then empress dowager.

literal: She held court and heard government, still styled "Your Highness" below the throne, and issued orders to conduct affairs.
idiomatic: She held court, still addressed as "Your Highness," and issued orders.

literal: Later orders were styled edicts; ministers' memorials addressed her as "Your Majesty," and she called herself "I, the ruler."
idiomatic: Later her orders were called edicts; ministers wrote "Your Majesty," and she used "I."

literal: The empress dowager, because Xiaozong was young and not yet able to sacrifice in person, wished to follow Zhou ritual's meaning of wife and lord mutually offering sacrifice and perform the rites in his stead, seeking former precedents.
idiomatic: Because Xiaozong was too young to sacrifice, she sought Zhou precedent for the consort's shared offering and meant to perform the rites herself.

literal: The Secretariat summoned ritual officers and academicians to debate; they deemed it impossible.
idiomatic: The Secretariat summoned ritualists and scholars, who ruled it impossible.

literal: Yet the empress dowager wished to screen herself with curtains and observe the Three Excellencies performing the rites, and questioned Attendant-in-ordinary Cui Guang again.
idiomatic: She wished to watch from behind a curtain as the Three Excellencies performed the rites and questioned Attendant-in-ordinary Cui Guang again.

literal: Guang promptly cited the Han precedent of Empress Dowager He and Xi of Deng recommending sacrifice; the empress dowager was greatly pleased and then acted in place for the first sacrifice.
idiomatic: Guang cited Empress Dowager Deng of Han; delighted, she performed the first sacrifice in the emperor's stead.

literal: The text is deficient.
idiomatic: The text is deficient.

literal: The empress dowager was clever and perceptive, with many talents; her aunt being a nun, they relied on each other from childhood and she grasped the great meaning of Buddhist sutras.
idiomatic: Clever and gifted, she had been raised by her nun aunt and grasped the gist of the sutras.

literal: She personally reviewed the myriad affairs of state and decided with her own hand.
idiomatic: She personally reviewed state affairs and wrote judgments herself.

literal: Visiting the Faliu Hall in Xilin Garden, she ordered attendant ministers to shoot; those who could not were punished.
idiomatic: At Faliu Hall in Xilin Garden she ordered ministers to shoot; failures were punished.

literal: She herself shot at a needle's eye and hit it.
idiomatic: She herself shot at a needle's eye and struck true.

literal: Greatly pleased, she bestowed cloth and silk on those around her in graded amounts.
idiomatic: Delighted, she gave graded gifts of cloth and silk to those around her.

literal: Earlier the empress dowager had ordered the construction of a petition carriage; she now rode it, going out from the Cloud Dragon grand marshal gate, circling northwest of the palace, entering by the Thousand Autumns gate to receive wrongful grievances.
idiomatic: She had built a petition carriage and rode it out the Cloud Dragon gate, around the palace's northwest, in by the Thousand Autumns gate to hear grievances.

literal: She also personally examined filial scholars and outstanding men and the commandery and district clerks at court.
idiomatic: She also examined filial scholars and provincial clerks in the hall of audience.

literal: The empress dowager and Xiaozong visited Hualin Garden, feasted the ministers at the winding water of the capital pavilion, and ordered princes, dukes, and below each to compose a seven-character verse poem.
idiomatic: With Xiaozong at Hualin Garden she feasted ministers at the winding stream and ordered each prince and official to compose a heptasyllabic poem.

literal: The empress dowager's poem said: "Transforming light creates things; holding qi, steadfast.
idiomatic: Her poem ran: "Transforming light creates things; holding breath, steadfast."

literal: " The emperor's poem said: "Respectfully restraining myself, inactive—I rely on kind excellence.
idiomatic: " The emperor's: "Respectfully at rest, I rely on kind excellence."

literal: " Princes, dukes, and below received graded gifts of cloth.
idiomatic: " Princes and officials below received graded gifts of cloth.

literal: The empress dowager's father died; the hundred officials memorialized requesting she leave office for mourning; the empress dowager did not permit it.
idiomatic: When her father died officials asked her to observe mourning; she refused.

literal: Soon she visited Yongning Temple and personally built a shrine on a nine-tier foundation; monks, nuns, gentlemen, and ladies who came numbered in the tens of thousands.
idiomatic: She visited Yongning Temple and built a shrine on a nine-tier base; tens of thousands of clergy and layfolk came.

literal: When Wenzhao Empress Gao was reburied, the empress dowager did not wish Xiaozong to preside; she herself became chief mourner, went out to Zhongning Mausoleum, personally offered the farewell rites, returned to weep at the Hall of Supreme Ultimate, and through completion presided over all.
idiomatic: At Wenzhao Empress Gao's reburial she would not let Xiaozong preside; she went to Zhongning as chief mourner, offered rites, wept at the Hall of Supreme Ultimate, and directed everything.

literal: Later she visited Mount Song; ladies, the nine concubines, princesses, and those below who followed numbered several hundred, ascending to the summit.
idiomatic: Later she climbed Mount Song with hundreds of consorts and princesses to the summit.

literal: She abolished various licentious sacrifices, but the Hu heavenly god was not among them.
idiomatic: She abolished illicit shrines but exempted the Hu heavenly cult.

literal: Later she visited the left treasury; princes, dukes, consorts, princesses, and those below who followed numbered more than a hundred—all were made to carry cloth and silk by their strength, then rewarded with it; the most received over two hundred bolts, the least more than a hundred.
idiomatic: At the left treasury she made over a hundred princes and ladies carry cloth and silk by strength, then gave it back—some over two hundred bolts, some over a hundred.

literal: Only Princess Changle came out holding twenty bolts of silk in her hands, showing she was not different from the crowd yet without toil.
idiomatic: Only Princess Changle carried out twenty bolts by hand, showing she matched the crowd without strain.

literal: The age praised her frugality.
idiomatic: The age praised her restraint.

literal: Equal in honor to the Three Excellencies, Duke of Chenliu Li Chong, and Prince of Zhangwu Rong both from carrying too much fell to the ground; Chong injured his waist, Rong even damaged his foot.
idiomatic: Li Chong, Duke of Chenliu, and Prince of Zhangwu Rong, bearing too much, fell—Chong hurt his back, Rong his leg.

literal: People of the time made a saying: "Chenliu and Zhangwu—hurt waist, broken thigh.
idiomatic: A rhyme ran: "Chenliu and Zhangwu—hurt back, broken leg.

literal: Greedy men ruin their kind and defile our enlightened lord.
idiomatic: Greedy men shame our bright sovereign."

literal: " Soon she visited the warm springs at Quekou, climbed Chicken Head Mountain, shot at an ivory hairpin herself, hit it with one shot, and ordered it shown to civil and military officials.
idiomatic: " She visited Quekou hot springs, climbed Chicken Head Mountain, shot an ivory hairpin at one cast, and displayed it to the court.

literal: By then the empress dowager had her will; she forced her favor on Prince of Qinghe Yi and indulged in lewd disorder at will, hated by the realm.
idiomatic: By then she forced herself on Prince of Qinghe Yi and indulged openly, hated throughout the realm.

literal: Director of the guards Yuan Cha, Director of the Long Autumn Liu Teng, and others installed Xiaozong in Xianyang Hall, confined the empress dowager in the northern palace, and killed Yi within the forbidden precinct.
idiomatic: Yuan Cha and Liu Teng installed Xiaozong in Xianyang Hall, confined her in the northern palace, and killed Yi inside the palace.

literal: Later the empress dowager's cousin Colonel-in-chief Sengjing and several dozen bodyguards including Zhang Chequ plotted to kill Cha and restore the empress dowager to court; it failed—Sengjing was banished to the frontier, Chequ and others died, and many of the Hu clan were dismissed.
idiomatic: Her cousin Sengjing and dozens of guards plotted to kill Cha and restore her; it failed—Sengjing was exiled, Chequ executed, many Hus dismissed.

literal: Later Xiaozong attended the empress dowager at Xilin Garden, feasted civil and military attendant ministers, and drank until evening.
idiomatic: Later Xiaozong visited her at Xilin Garden and feasted ministers until evening.

literal: Cha then rose before the empress dowager and, speaking outward, claimed the empress dowager wished to harm him and Teng.
idiomatic: Cha rose before her and declared aloud that she meant to kill him and Teng.

literal: The empress dowager answered that there was no such talk.
idiomatic: She answered that she had said no such thing.

literal: It then reached extreme confusion.
idiomatic: Matters descended into utter chaos.

literal: The empress dowager then rose, took Xiaozong's hand, and left the hall, saying: "Mother and son have not gathered long; tonight we shall lodge together—ministers, escort me in.
idiomatic: She took Xiaozong's hand and left, saying: "Mother and son have been apart too long—we lodge together tonight; ministers, see me in.

literal: " The empress dowager and Xiaozong went to a small chamber in the northeast; Left Guard General Xi Kangsheng plotted to kill Cha but did not succeed.
idiomatic: " They went to a northeast chamber; Left Guard General Xi Kangsheng plotted to kill Cha but failed.

literal: After Liu Teng died, Cha again grew lax and negligent.
idiomatic: After Liu Teng's death Cha grew lax again.

literal: The empress dowager, Xiaozong, and Prince of Gaoyang Yong plotted together and removed Cha from the directorship of the guards.
idiomatic: She, Xiaozong, and Prince of Gaoyang Yong plotted and stripped Cha of the guards command.

literal: The empress dowager again held court, proclaimed a great amnesty, and changed the era name.
idiomatic: She returned to court, proclaimed a great amnesty, and changed the reign title.

literal: From then government grew slack, authority and favor were not established, and prefects and shepherds everywhere were greedy.
idiomatic: Thereafter government slackened, authority waned, and local officials grew greedy everywhere.

literal: Zheng Yan defiled the inner palace; his power tilted the seas within.
idiomatic: Zheng Yan defiled the inner palace and his power tilted the realm;

literal: Li Shengui and Xu He were both received in close attendance.
idiomatic: Li Shengui and Xu He enjoyed intimate attendance.

literal: Within a year or two they held posts summing the forbidden core, grasped princely seals in their hands, weight and lightness lay in their hearts, proclaimed lewdness at court, and were loathed and defiled by the four quarters.
idiomatic: Within a year or two they held the palace's keys, grasped princely seals, ruled by whim, flaunted lust at court, and were loathed in every quarter.

literal: Civil and military offices dissolved; rebellion rose everywhere—earth collapsing, fish rotting—from this it came.
idiomatic: Civil and military order collapsed, rebellion spread everywhere—the realm crumbled from this.

literal: Sengjing again, gathering kin, wept and remonstrated: "Your Majesty, motherly model of the seas within—how can you cast restraint aside so lightly!
idiomatic: Sengjing gathered kin and wept in remonstrance: "Your Majesty, model of motherhood for the realm—how can you cast restraint aside so lightly!

literal: " The empress was greatly angry and from then did not summon Sengjing.
idiomatic: " She flew into a rage and never summoned Sengjing again.

literal: The empress dowager, considering her conduct unreformed, feared resentment from the imperial clan; she therefore formed factions within, blocked ears and eyes, and many whom Xiaozong favored the empress dowager harmed on one pretext or another.
idiomatic: Knowing her conduct was shameful and fearing the clan, she formed factions, sealed off news, and destroyed many Xiaozong favored.
